paragraphs: Policy gradient methods improve a reinforcement learning policy by following a direction that increases its objective. Their theoretical foundation is well established when the policy being improved also produces the training experience. Off-policy learning separates these roles: experience can come from a different behavior policy, making the corresponding gradient calculation more difficult.

The paper provides an off-policy policy gradient theorem using emphatic weightings. These weightings are the key mathematical ingredient that makes a simplified gradient expression possible in this setting. The authors then translate the theorem into Actor Critic with Emphatic weightings, or ACE, an algorithm that approximates the gradients supplied by the result.

A simple counterexample illustrates why the distinction matters. In that example, earlier methods, specifically OffPAC and DPG, converge to an incorrect solution, while ACE reaches the optimum. This is a targeted demonstration of a theoretical problem and its proposed correction, rather than evidence that ACE universally outperforms those methods. The central contribution is a principled foundation for off-policy policy improvement.
neurips-2018-an-off-policy-policy-gradie.tldr: An off-policy policy gradient theorem based on emphatic weightings leads to ACE, which corrects failures demonstrated in a simple counterexample.

paragraphs: Clustering groups users or data points according to a service or similarity objective. This paper studies stochastic versions of clustering, where the solution is evaluated with randomness taken into account. The authors develop approximation algorithms for several such formulations, giving mathematical guarantees about how close their solutions come to the relevant optimum.

One stated benefit is better approximation ratios than those available in the usual deterministic setting. Randomness also changes how service can be distributed among users. The algorithms provide guarantees of good service on average for every user, connecting clustering quality to individual long-term outcomes. An average guarantee concerns performance across the randomness; it does not promise the same service quality in every individual outcome.

The paper therefore treats stochastic clustering as a way to improve both approximation guarantees and fairness of service. It also establishes impossibility results for some of the settings, placing boundaries around what algorithms can achieve. Together, the positive and negative results clarify both the advantages of these stochastic formulations and the limits of their guarantees.
neurips-2018-approximation-algorithms-fo.tldr: Stochastic clustering algorithms offer improved approximation guarantees and good average service for every user, alongside impossibility results.

paragraphs: Learning personalized decisions from observational data is difficult when hidden factors influence both the treatment someone receives and their outcome. Such confounding can make a policy look beneficial for reasons that do not reflect its actual effects. This paper builds policy learning around possible violations of the assumption that no such hidden factors exist.

The method represents uncertainty through sets around nominal propensity weights, drawing on causal sensitivity analysis. It chooses a candidate policy by optimizing its worst-case regret relative to a reference policy across that uncertainty set. The reference policy gives improvement a concrete meaning: the new decisions are judged against an existing status quo.

The safety guarantee is conditional on the uncertainty set being well specified. Under that condition, the learned policy can do no worse than the baseline and improves only when the data supports improvement. The authors develop efficient optimization methods for parameterized policies and assess them on synthetic data and a large clinical trial. Their results illustrate how confounded selection can cause harmful policy choices and how robust optimization can focus decisions on supported gains.
neurips-2018-confounding-robust-policy-i.tldr: A robust policy-learning framework protects against worsening a baseline when its uncertainty set correctly captures possible unobserved confounding.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned account of an environment's dynamics to support decision making. It can learn from relatively little experience, but its eventual performance often falls below that of strong model-free methods, particularly when deep networks represent the dynamics. This paper investigates whether explicitly handling uncertainty can narrow that gap.

The proposed algorithm, probabilistic ensembles with trajectory sampling, or PETS, combines uncertainty-aware deep dynamics models with sampling-based propagation of uncertainty. The approach carries uncertainty through predicted trajectories rather than relying only on a single forecast of what will happen. This connects the representation of uncertainty in the model to its use during decision making.

On several challenging benchmark tasks, the reported comparisons show PETS matching the eventual performance of model-free algorithms while using substantially fewer samples. On half-cheetah, the abstract reports eight times fewer samples than Soft Actor Critic and 125 times fewer than Proximal Policy Optimization. These results show that, on the evaluated tasks, strong final performance and efficient use of experience can coexist within a model-based approach.
neurips-2018-deep-reinforcement-learning.tldr: PETS combines uncertainty-aware dynamics models and trajectory sampling to match model-free performance on several benchmarks using far fewer samples.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a way to compare distributions, and entropic regularization has made its computation more practical. In learning applications, however, obtaining gradients is also important. The paper addresses a common substitution: replacing the original Sinkhorn approximation to Wasserstein distance with a less accurate regularized version because that alternative is easier to differentiate.

The authors characterize the differential properties of the original approximation and prove that it has the same smoothness as the regularized version. They also give an efficient algorithm for computing its gradient. Together, these results address both the mathematical question of whether suitable derivatives exist and the computational question of how to obtain them.

The consequences extend in two directions. Higher-order smoothness supports statistical guarantees for learning with Wasserstein approximations, while the gradient formula makes practical learning and optimization possible with the original approximation. The paper includes promising preliminary experiments, so its empirical evidence is presented as an initial complement to the analysis. Its main contribution is establishing the properties and computational tools needed to use this approximation more directly.
neurips-2018-differential-properties-of-.tldr: The original Sinkhorn approximation has the same smoothness as its regularized alternative and admits efficient gradient computation.

paragraphs: A predictor trained in one setting may encounter a different distribution when deployed elsewhere. This paper studies cases where those settings can be understood as different contexts of the same underlying system. Their differences are modeled as perturbations, or interventions in causal language, providing a structured account of why the distributions change.

The task is to use data from one or more source domains to predict the distribution of a target variable from other measurements in one or more target domains. The proposed approach uses causal inference to address this transfer problem. It does not require prior knowledge of the causal graph, the kinds of interventions, or which variables the interventions affect.

This matters because those causal details may be unavailable even when several contexts share an underlying system. The approach applies to the class of causal domain adaptation problems studied, rather than establishing a solution for arbitrary distribution changes. The authors evaluate one possible implementation on simulated and real-world data, demonstrating how the proposed causal perspective can be put into practice.
neurips-2018-domain-adaptation-by-using-.tldr: A causal approach transfers predictions across intervention-related domains without requiring prior knowledge of their causal graph or interventions.

paragraphs: Stopping an iterative learning algorithm before it fully fits the data is a familiar way to control overfitting. This paper studies early stopping for a different statistical goal: hypothesis testing in a general nonparametric setting. The question is whether the number of optimization steps can be chosen to obtain the best possible testing performance in a minimax sense.

The authors construct a Wald-type test from an estimate produced by functional gradient descent in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Their central result gives a sharp rule for when to stop. Testing optimality is achievable when the iteration count has the required optimal order, and becomes impossible when that order is not met within the analyzed setting.

The stopping time therefore plays a fundamental statistical role, beyond saving computation or serving as a practical heuristic. The paper also derives a related sharpness result for optimal estimation under early stopping. The analysis covers multiple kernel classes, including Sobolev smoothness and Gaussian kernels, showing that the relationship between iteration count and statistical optimality extends across these function classes.
neurips-2018-early-stopping-for-nonparam.tldr: A sharp early-stopping rule makes minimax-optimal nonparametric testing achievable and identifies iteration orders where optimality is impossible.

paragraphs: Object localization identifies where an object lies, while segmentation identifies the image regions belonging to it. This paper combines the two tasks in a single optimization problem under very weak supervision. It brings together appearance information at a low level and localization information at a higher level, allowing each representation to inform the other.

The framework connects bounding boxes with superpixels through linear constraints that express their spatial relationships. It simultaneously distinguishes foreground from background at both levels. A foreground model additionally encourages an object's appearance histograms to remain similar across frames. This supplies a source of consistency beyond the discriminative clustering used by earlier approaches.

That addition is particularly relevant to video, where similar backgrounds across frames may provide little discriminative information. The geometric connection lets segmentation cues improve localization and localization cues improve segmentation. Evaluations on the YouTube Object video dataset, Internet Object Discovery dataset, and Pascal VOC 2007 demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is a unified way to combine spatial agreement and foreground appearance across the two tasks.
neurips-2018-foreground-clustering-for-j.tldr: A joint optimization framework links bounding boxes, superpixels, and foreground appearance to improve segmentation and localization together.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic optimization can involve delayed information, multiple workers, and communication that happens only intermittently. These arrangements differ in which computations can depend on which earlier results. The paper introduces an oracle-based framework that represents those dependencies with a graph, giving different parallelization settings a shared mathematical description.

Using this representation, the authors derive generic lower bounds in terms of the dependency graph. Such bounds describe unavoidable demands on oracle access within the modeled setting. They then apply the framework to particular cases, including delayed updates and parallel processing with intermittent communication, to study how those structures constrain optimization.

The analysis also compares lower bounds with available upper bounds on oracle complexity. Gaps between them mark places where current guarantees do not settle the best achievable performance. In some cases, algorithms that appear to be natural choices are not known to be optimal. The paper's value is both a reusable framework for analyzing parallel optimization and a clearer identification of unresolved questions about algorithm quality.
neurips-2018-graph-oracle-models-lower-b.tldr: Dependency graphs provide a common framework for lower bounds in parallel stochastic optimization and expose gaps in known algorithm guarantees.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through events over time, making their training difficult because spikes are discontinuous and their dynamics are complex. Existing backpropagation approaches can have scalability problems or compute gradients that do not match the rate-coded training objective. This paper introduces hybrid macro/micro level backpropagation, called HM2-BP, to address these issues.

At the microscopic level, a spike-train-level postsynaptic potential represents temporal effects. At the macroscopic level, errors are defined through firing rates. The algorithm propagates these errors across both levels and directly computes gradients of the rate-coded loss with respect to adjustable parameters. This links the chosen training objective to the detailed temporal behavior of the network.

The authors evaluate fully connected and convolutional spiking networks. Reported accuracies reach 99.49% on MNIST and 98.88% on N-MNIST, exceeding the previously reported spiking backpropagation results they compare against. They also report strong results on EMNIST and spoken-letter recognition using TI46. For asynchronous spike streams, the reported performance surpasses conventional deep learning models in the evaluated comparisons.
neurips-2018-hybrid-macro-micro-level-ba.tldr: HM2-BP connects spike timing and rate-coded errors to directly train deep spiking networks, with strong reported image and speech recognition results.

paragraphs: Some large optimization problems have structure expressed through a Riemannian manifold, so the optimization algorithm must respect that geometry. Riemannian trust-region methods are a popular approach to such problems. This paper develops an inexact version aimed at structured problems involving large datasets, where computing all the ingredients of an update can be expensive.

The proposed method approximates the gradient, the Hessian, and the solution of the trust-region subproblem. For finite-sum objectives, the authors use random sampling to compute approximate gradients and Hessians. They specifically propose algorithms with fixed bounds on the numbers of samples used for those two computations, limiting how much data those derivative calculations draw on.

The approach makes approximation part of several stages of the optimization procedure, allowing the method to work with reduced computational inputs while retaining the manifold-based formulation. Numerical evaluations across different applications show the proposed algorithms outperforming the state-of-the-art deterministic and stochastic Riemannian gradient methods considered. The stated evidence supports their practical value for the evaluated large-scale optimization problems.
neurips-2018-inexact-trust-region-algori.tldr: Inexact Riemannian trust-region algorithms use sampled derivatives and approximate subproblem solutions to improve performance on evaluated large-scale problems.

paragraphs: Distributing neural network training by splitting a batch is convenient, but it can leave model size constrained by memory and become inefficient with small batches. More general model parallelism can address these problems, yet efficient implementations are difficult to specify on large clusters. Mesh-TensorFlow introduces a language for describing a broad class of distributed tensor computations.

Users specify which tensor dimensions are divided across which dimensions of a processor mesh. This extends distribution beyond the batch dimension to other parts of the computation. The resulting graph compiles into a single-program, multiple-data implementation, combining parallel operations with collective communication such as Allreduce. The language provides a way to express how computation is distributed while compilation produces the corresponding program.

The authors demonstrate the approach with a Transformer that combines data and model parallelism. Using TPU meshes with up to 512 cores, they train models containing up to five billion parameters. They report surpassing the then-state-of-the-art results on English-to-French translation and a billion-word language modeling benchmark, demonstrating the system's ability to support large, effective models.
neurips-2018-mesh-tensorflow-deep-learni.tldr: Mesh-TensorFlow lets users distribute tensor dimensions across processor meshes and demonstrates large-scale Transformer training with combined data and model parallelism.

paragraphs: Generating detailed three-dimensional objects becomes costly when a model works directly with high-resolution voxel volumes. This paper approaches that scaling problem through six orthographic depth views of each object. Networks increase the resolution of those two-dimensional projections, enabling fast upsampling of the object in voxel space with more efficient scaling than direct three-dimensional methods.

The method further divides depth super-resolution into silhouette prediction and depth prediction. These components address the object's structure and its finer surface detail. The authors report that this decomposition makes sharp edges easier to generate than using a single network, connecting a representational choice to the quality of the reconstructed geometry.

Across experiments with high-resolution objects, the system accurately predicts novel objects at resolutions reaching 512 by 512 by 512, described as the highest reported resolution for the task. The authors also report state-of-the-art reconstruction from RGB images on ShapeNet and present what they describe as the first effective three-dimensional super-resolution method. The results support using coordinated two-dimensional views to make detailed three-dimensional modeling more practical.
neurips-2018-multi-view-silhouette-and-d.tldr: Super-resolving six depth views, with separate silhouette and depth predictions, enables efficient high-resolution three-dimensional object reconstruction.

paragraphs: Looking several steps ahead can support strong reinforcement learning decisions, as illustrated by Monte Carlo Tree Search and Model Predictive Control. Earlier work had analyzed multiple-step greedy policies in basic policy iteration. This paper investigates their use in more practical settings involving online learning and approximations, where the way a policy is updated becomes especially important.

The authors identify a counterintuitive problem with soft policy updates, which move only partway toward a new policy. With a multiple-step greedy policy, such updates do not guarantee monotonic improvement unless the update step is sufficiently large. The difficulty can arise even without approximation errors, so it cannot be attributed solely to inaccurate estimates.

This distinguishes the multiple-step case from the one-step greedy setting and challenges the intuition that a smaller update is necessarily a safer improvement. Taking this issue into account, the paper formulates and analyzes online and approximate algorithms using a multiple-step greedy operator. The contribution is an analysis of how deeper lookahead interacts with policy updates, together with algorithms designed around that interaction.
neurips-2018-multiple-step-greedy-polici.tldr: Multiple-step greedy policies can lose monotonic improvement under small soft updates, motivating carefully analyzed online and approximate algorithms.

paragraphs: An MDP's specified state space can contain transient states or configurations that no policy can reach. Such states create difficulties for exploration methods that effectively expect all states to communicate. The paper introduces TUCRL, described as the first algorithm to support efficient exploration and exploitation in any finite MDP without requiring prior knowledge.

Its regret bound grows with the square root of interaction time and depends on the size, transition connectivity, and diameter of the communicating portion of the MDP. This focuses the guarantee on the relevant connected structure. The authors contrast it with optimistic approaches that can incur linear regret in weakly communicating settings and other approaches that need prior information about the optimal policy's bias span.

The paper also establishes a fundamental obstacle: logarithmic regret growth in weakly communicating MDPs cannot be achieved without first enduring a linear-regret period whose length is exponential in MDP parameters. Numerical simulations support the analysis and demonstrate how TUCRL addresses limitations of existing methods. The findings combine an algorithmic advance with a bound on what stronger exploration guarantees can demand.
neurips-2018-near-optimal-exploration-ex.tldr: TUCRL provides efficient exploration without prior knowledge in finite MDPs, with regret tied to their communicating structure.

paragraphs: Unsupervised cross-domain mapping seeks a mapping between domains without supervision. Much of the progress discussed in this paper relies on adversarial training and cycle constraints. Because adversarial training can be difficult in practice, the authors investigate a different route based on a new form of variational autoencoder.

Their starting point is earlier evidence that mapping across domains can work without cycles or generative adversarial networks. That earlier approach has practical costs: inference is expensive, and it assigns a separate optimization variable to every training example. The latter requirement prevents it from making use of large training sets, creating a scaling problem in addition to the cost of applying the trained method.

The proposed variational-autoencoder approach achieves non-adversarial mapping while addressing those stated drawbacks. The authors report much faster inference, the ability to use large datasets, and a simple interpretation. These claims make the contribution primarily about the practicality of non-adversarial mapping: a promising alternative becomes easier to apply and better able to benefit from more training data.
neurips-2018-non-adversarial-mapping-wit.tldr: A new variational-autoencoder approach enables non-adversarial cross-domain mapping with faster inference and support for large datasets.

paragraphs: A differentially private mechanism can provide stronger privacy when applied to a random subsample than when applied to the entire population. This principle, called privacy amplification by subsampling, is useful when designing private analyses. Previous treatments had established particular versions of the principle for different sampling procedures through separate, specialized arguments.

The paper develops a general analysis method that recovers earlier results, improves some of them, and derives new instances of amplification. It also produces lower bounds. Combining guarantees with lower bounds helps characterize both the privacy improvement that can be established and the limits on how strong an analysis can be.

The method uses a characterization of differential privacy in terms of a divergence, drawing on ideas from program verification. It introduces additional mathematical tools, including advanced joint convexity and privacy profiles, that the authors suggest may have independent value. The main contribution is a common analytical foundation for several subsampling settings, reducing reliance on disconnected proofs while enabling stronger and broader results.
neurips-2018-privacy-amplification-by-su.tldr: A general divergence-based framework unifies and strengthens privacy amplification analyses for random subsampling while also providing lower bounds.

paragraphs: Machine learning often optimizes a convenient surrogate loss in place of the task's original loss. A convex surrogate can simplify optimization, but an inconsistent surrogate does not fully align its optimum with the desired task objective. This paper asks how useful learning guarantees can still be established when that mismatch is present.

The authors extend a quantitative consistency framework to inconsistent surrogates. Their main technical result is a lower bound on the calibration function for the quadratic surrogate that can remain informative in inconsistent cases, instead of always collapsing to zero. The bound quantifies the degree of inconsistency and supports guarantees concerning sample complexity and optimization difficulty.

The theory is applied to multiclass classification with a tree-structured loss and ranking with mean average precision loss. These examples expose a tradeoff between approximation quality and computational considerations. The findings show why inconsistency alone need not make a surrogate useless: its mismatch can be measured, and useful guarantees can remain available. The potential benefits depend on the resulting approximation-computation tradeoff.
neurips-2018-quantifying-learning-guaran.tldr: A new calibration bound quantifies how inconsistent quadratic surrogates can still offer learning guarantees and useful approximation-computation tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Laplacian K-modes combines clustering with finding density modes, which represent concentrated regions of the data. This paper proposes a concave-convex relaxation that makes the problem amenable to parallel computation. Its optimizer works through a tight auxiliary bound, producing an independent update for each cluster-assignment variable at every iteration with guaranteed convergence.

Those independent updates make distribution across processors straightforward. The formulation avoids storing a full affinity matrix, performing its eigendecomposition, and using costly projection or dual inner iterations for each point's constraints. Density modes are extracted from the assignment variables through maximum-value operations, adding computational work that is linear in the number of data points.

The mode-estimation procedure also avoids the inner gradient-ascent iterations used by mean-shift. Its complexity is independent of feature-space dimension, its returned modes are actual input points, and it supports discrete domains and arbitrary kernels. Experiments across multiple datasets report competitive clustering accuracy and optimization quality. These results support a formulation that makes joint clustering and mode finding more scalable without requiring those expensive intermediate operations.
neurips-2018-scalable-laplacian-k-modes-.tldr: A parallel relaxation of Laplacian K-modes scales clustering and density-mode finding through independent assignment updates and inexpensive mode extraction.

paragraphs: Recording hundreds or thousands of neurons simultaneously produces datasets that strain conventional statistical analysis. This paper develops approximate inference for Poisson generalized linear models that requires only one pass through the data. It adapts polynomial approximations to construct approximate sufficient statistics, providing a more scalable basis for fitting models of neural spike counts.

The authors focus on quadratic approximations to nonlinear log-likelihood terms, together with Gaussian priors. This yields closed-form expressions for approximate maximum-likelihood and maximum-a-posteriori estimates, the posterior distribution, and marginal likelihood. An adaptive procedure selects the interval over which the polynomial approximation is built. The resulting method supports efficient, accurate inference and regularization of high-dimensional parameters.

The authors demonstrate the method by fitting a fully coupled model to recordings from 831 neurons across five mouse brain regions. The recordings span 41 minutes at one-millisecond resolution, totaling more than two billion spike-count bins across neurons. The fitted model identifies fine-timescale statistical dependencies within and across cortical and subcortical areas, showing the scale of neural relationships this approximation makes practical to analyze.
neurips-2018-scaling-the-poisson-glm-to-.tldr: Quadratic approximations enable single-pass Poisson GLM inference at the scale of billions of neural spike-count bins.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced clustering can use judgments about whether two examples belong in the same group. Those judgments may be noisy and available for only a small part of the dataset. This paper combines that limited relational supervision with a deep generative model of the data, allowing both sources of information to contribute to clustering.

One component models low-level data features, while a statistical relational component models the noisy pairwise annotations. They share latent variables, linking the explanations they develop for the observations and the annotations. The authors also introduce a fully Bayesian version intended to automatically balance model complexity against how well the model fits the available data.

Inference combines variational message passing for the relational component with amortized learning for the generative component. Natural-gradient stochastic variational inference provides a unified computational approach to learning the combined model. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the reported method outperforms previous crowdsourced clustering approaches. The findings support jointly modeling data structure and annotation noise when only limited pairwise supervision is available.
neurips-2018-semi-crowdsourced-clusterin.tldr: A shared latent-variable model combines deep generative learning with noisy crowd judgments to improve semi-supervised clustering.

paragraphs: Music generation often uses scores or MIDI, which capture musical events while abstracting away details of an individual performance. This paper works directly with raw audio to retain nuances that matter for perceived realism and musicality. Doing so requires a model to handle both the immediate waveform and musical relationships extending over much longer periods.

The authors find that autoregressive models, despite their success with speech waveforms, favor local signal structure when applied to music. That emphasis comes at the expense of long-range correlations. Since music contains organization at many timescales, accurately modeling nearby audio samples alone does not address the full generation problem.

The paper explores autoregressive discrete autoencoders as a way to help autoregressive models capture those longer relationships. The resulting system generates piano music unconditionally in the raw audio domain, with reported stylistic consistency lasting tens of seconds. This finding supports the proposed representation as a way to extend coherence beyond short waveform patterns, while preserving the paper's focus on the demonstrated piano-generation setting.
neurips-2018-the-challenge-of-realistic-.tldr: Autoregressive discrete autoencoders enable raw-audio piano generation with reported stylistic consistency across tens of seconds.

paragraphs: Deep networks can contain more parameters than training observations and still perform well. This paper examines that apparent puzzle through compression: how compactly can the data be encoded when the cost of describing the network's parameters is included? The relevant quantity is the full description length, rather than the parameter count by itself.

The experiments show that deep networks can provide lossless data compression even after accounting for parameter encoding. This establishes that a large parameter count need not prevent a model from giving a compact description of the data. The paper also examines variational methods, whose motivation includes optimizing compression-related bounds, and finds their bounds surprisingly poor.

Encoding techniques drawn from Minimum Description Length yield substantially better compression values for the deep networks studied. This makes the choice of encoding method important when assessing a model through description length. The authors suggest that weak compression bounds might help explain the relatively poor practical performance of variational methods, but present that connection as a possible explanation rather than an established causal result.
neurips-2018-the-description-length-of-d.tldr: Deep networks can compress data losslessly despite parameter-encoding costs, and MDL encoding methods provide better compression values than the studied variational bounds.

paragraphs: Many interpretability methods explain individual predictions after a model has already been trained. This paper instead makes explanation quality part of model design and learning. It identifies three desired properties: explanations should be explicit, faithful to the model, and stable. The authors show that existing methods fail to satisfy these requirements.

The proposed models are constructed by progressively extending linear classifiers into more complex architectures that retain an explicit explanatory structure. Tailored regularization is used to enforce faithfulness and stability. This connects the model's predictive behavior and its explanations during training, rather than relying entirely on a separate procedure to interpret a finished predictor.

Experiments across several benchmark datasets support the framework as a promising approach to combining complexity with interpretability. The stated result is a direction for reconciling those goals, rather than a universal resolution of explanation quality. The contribution lies in turning desired explanation properties into architectural and training choices, giving interpretability a concrete role in how a neural network is built and learned.
neurips-2018-towards-robust-interpretabi.tldr: Self-explaining neural networks build explicit explanations into their architecture and use regularization to promote faithfulness and stability.

paragraphs: Unsupervised text style transfer needs a training signal that encourages generated sentences to resemble language in a target domain. Binary discriminators can provide too little feedback to teach richly structured language. This paper replaces that discriminator with a target-domain language model, which supplies feedback at the level of individual tokens.

The generator minimizes the negative log likelihood of its generated sentences under the language model. Because the language model scores a sentence through locally normalized token probabilities, its feedback reflects more of the sentence's structure. A continuous approximation to discrete samples allows the complete system to be trained through backpropagation.

The authors also find empirically that this structured discriminator can eliminate adversarial training steps involving negative samples, making training more stable. Comparisons with earlier methods using convolutional discriminators show significant improvements on word-substitution decipherment, sentiment modification, and related-language translation. The results support richer language-model feedback as both a useful learning signal and a way to simplify training in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-text-style-tra.tldr: Using a language model as a discriminator gives token-level feedback that improves unsupervised text transfer and can simplify adversarial training.
